questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Singular Values of a Matrix
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- Any $3\times 2$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
- The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -1 & -5\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value.
- Any $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $2\times 2$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{2\times 3}\times {A}_{3\times 2}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{2\times 2}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 2}\times {A}_{2\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Rechecking confirms I and III are true: A^T A has size 2×2 for I and 3×3 for III, giving at most 2 and 3 distinct singular values, respectively. Having at most 2 also implies having at most 3. II is false because singular values cannot be negative. The earlier uncertainty arises from the missing choice “I and III only”; none of the displayed options is valid.

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- Any matrix of the form  $A=[\begin{aligned}-a & 0 \\ 0 & a\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value.
- Any $5\times 2$ matrix $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.
- Any $4\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false.  All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, 
$A$  can't have any negative singular value.

- Statement II is false. Since $A$ is a $5\times 2$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $2\times 5$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $2\times 2$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{2\times 5}\times {A}_{5\times 2}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{2\times 2}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed,  since $A$ is a $4\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Rechecking: I is false since A^T A=a^2 I, so both singular values equal |a| and are nonnegative. II is true: A^T A is 2×2, giving at most 2 distinct singular values, hence at most 5. III is true: A^T A is 5×5, giving at most 5 distinct singular values. The earlier uncertainty is due to the missing combination “II and III only.” Every displayed option is incorrect.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix
questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \,\,-1 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 2-\lambda  \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(2-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(2-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-1) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (2-\lambda )^{2} & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,2,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix
questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -6 \\ -6 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & -6 \\ -6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )(10-\lambda )-36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +100-36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +64 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda -16) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =16,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{16}=4 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}0 & 4-\lambda  \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )((4-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(20-4\lambda -5\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-16)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4-4) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -4)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- Any $1\times4$ matrix $A$ has at most $1$ singular value.

- Any $4\times2$ matrix $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- The matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14078642/assets/a33b8a531dc91b49f01826cd7fcedaae2ee3144b5205bbe724efa9f29a302b37.png) has one negative singular value.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $1 \times 4$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $4\times 1$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $4 \times 4$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times {\large 1}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 1} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A} =  
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Since $A$ is a $4 \times 2$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 4}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ cannot have a negative singular value.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."
